straight_leg_raise.emg_notes: Psoas >60% MVIC at end-range; rectus femoris 40-50% MVIC [Okubo 2021]
straight_leg_raise.dosing_recommendation: 3×10-15 reps per leg; progress with ankle weights

mini_squats.emg_notes: Quad 40-70% MVIC; glute max increases with depth: partial 16.9%, parallel 28.0%, full 35.4% [Caterisano 2002]

terminal_knee_extension.emg_notes: VM and VL significantly more active during last 15° extension [Gryzlo 1994]
terminal_knee_extension.dosing_recommendation: 3×15-20 reps; focus on last 15° of extension

romanian_deadlift.emg_notes: Comparative surface-EMG studies of hamstring exercises consistently show the Romanian deadlift produces high activation of the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus, in the same tier as the good morning and glute-ham raise, with hamstring activity typically greatest during the eccentric-to-concentric transition near peak hip flexion. Relative to knee-flexion-dominant exercises (leg curl, Nordic curl), the RDL biases hip-extension-based hamstring loading and tends to emphasize the biceps femoris long head somewhat more than the semitendinosus. Erector spinae activity is substantial but predominantly isometric when a neutral spine is maintained. Gluteus maximus activation rises toward lockout as the hip approaches full extension.
romanian_deadlift.dosing_recommendation: Strength/hypertrophy: 3-4 sets of 6-10 reps at a controlled tempo, 1-2 sessions per week. For hamstring injury-risk reduction, eccentric-biased hinge work at long muscle lengths is commonly programmed 1-2x/week alongside (not replacing) high-eccentric exercises such as the Nordic hamstring curl.

clamshell.emg_notes: Glute med 26-67% MVIC; highest glute med-to-TFL ratio (115) among exercises [Selkowitz 2013]; 60° hip flexion optimal [Willcox 2013]

hip_thrust.body_position: supine-inclined (upper back supported on bench, feet on floor)
hip_thrust.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies (notably work by Contreras and colleagues) consistently show very high gluteus maximus activation during the barbell hip thrust, with peak activity at terminal hip extension — often exceeding that measured in the back squat at comparable relative loads, since the horizontal loading vector keeps the hip-extension moment high at lockout. Biceps femoris and vastus lateralis show moderate activity, with hamstring contribution increasing as feet move further from the hips and quadriceps contribution increasing as feet move closer. Longitudinal training studies suggest the hip thrust and squat produce broadly comparable gluteal hypertrophy, so its main distinction is the activation profile and end-range emphasis rather than proven superior growth.
hip_thrust.dosing_recommendation: For strength/hypertrophy: 3-4 sets of 6-12 reps, 2-3 times per week, with progressive loading — consistent with general resistance-training guidelines; no hip-thrust-specific dosing standard exists.

spanish_squat.emg_notes: No specific Spanish squat EMG data. General CKC squats: VMO:VL approaching 1:1 [Chen 2018]. PF forces reduced 14.4% with decreased knee flexion [Kernozek 2020]
spanish_squat.dosing_recommendation: 3×15-30 reps, 0-60° knee flexion, 3-5 days/week for 6-12 weeks [APTA 2020, Neal 2024]

lateral_bounds.emg_notes: Peak forces 3.31 BW, RFD 0.94 BW/s [Wong 2012]. Glute med critical for frontal plane control [Maniar 2022]
lateral_bounds.dosing_recommendation: 2-3×6-10 reps per leg, 2x/week. Progress distance, height, and direction changes [Wong 2012]

sit_to_stand.dosing_recommendation: 3×10 reps, daily; progress to 5×STS timed test

pendulum_exercise.dosing_recommendation: 5-10 minutes, 2-3x daily; small circles in both directions, forward/back, and side-to-side. With or without 1-2 lb weight [expert consensus]

lateral_raises.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of common shoulder exercises consistently show the lateral (middle) deltoid is highly active during dumbbell lateral raises — typically among the highest of common free-weight shoulder exercises for that head, generally exceeding its activation during overhead pressing. The supraspinatus is also substantially active, working with the deltoid throughout abduction rather than only in the first degrees. Anterior and posterior deltoid activity is moderate and shifts with the plane of the raise: moving into scaption biases the anterior deltoid, while staying behind the frontal plane biases the posterior fibers. Upper trapezius activity rises with the arm, particularly above roughly 60-80 degrees, and increases further if the lifter shrugs or uses momentum. Mechanically the exercise loads the deltoid most near shoulder height where the load's moment arm is longest, which is why cable variants (constant tension at the bottom) feel harder early in the range. No specific citations are attached; this summary reflects the general pattern of published EMG comparisons of deltoid exercises.
lateral_raises.dosing_recommendation: Common practice for strengthening/hypertrophy: 2-4 sets of 8-15 repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, with load selected so the last 2-3 reps are challenging while form (no trunk swing or shrug) is maintained. This follows general resistance-training guidelines rather than lateral-raise-specific trials.

full_can_exercise.emg_notes: Supraspinatus: similar to empty can; middle deltoid: 52±27% MVIC (vs 77±44% in empty can, p=0.001). Superior supraspinatus-to-deltoid ratio [Reinold 2008]
full_can_exercise.dosing_recommendation: 3×15 reps, 1-2x daily for 12 weeks; or progressive resistance 5 days/week over 12-16 weeks [Holmgren 2012, GRASP 2021]

push_up_plus.emg_notes: High serratus anterior activation with favorable LT/UT ratio [Andersen 2012, Kibler 2008]

overhead_press.emg_notes: Anterior deltoid 60-90% MVIC; middle deltoid 50-80% MVIC; standing increases activation 8-15% [Saeterbakken 2013]

begin_when_fwb_pain_free_and_strength.canonical_name: Initiate When FWB Pain-Free and Sufficient Strength

cat_camel.emg_notes: Multifidus 9.7-16.9% MVIC during lordosis (cow) phase [Shah 2020]. Low-level activation appropriate for early motor control training.

diaphragmatic_breathing.emg_notes: Improves chest expansion, spinal mobility, and posture comparably to yoga/Pilates [Csepregi 2022]
diaphragmatic_breathing.dosing_recommendation: 10 breaths × 3 sets, 2-3x daily; 4-count inhale, 6-8 count exhale

bird_dog.emg_notes: Glute max ~40-56% MVIC; erector spinae 29% nEMG; lowest L/G ratio (1.21) indicating good local muscle targeting [Ekstrom 2007, Khosrokiani 2021]
bird_dog.dosing_recommendation: 3×8-10 reps per side with 5-10 second holds

bridge.emg_notes: Glute max 20-40% MVIC; hamstrings 15-25% MVIC; single-leg variation significantly increases activation [Ekstrom 2007, Hirose 2018]

side_plank.emg_notes: QL 121.62% MVIC, glute med 66.67% MVIC [Nam 2025]. Rotational variant: EO 62.8%, RA 43.9%, glute med >69% [Youdas 2014]
side_plank.dosing_recommendation: 3×15-30 second holds per side, progress to 45-60 seconds; 2-3x/week

pallof_press.emg_notes: Limited specific EMG data. General anti-rotation exercises activate obliques and core stabilizers. Motor control exercise SMD -0.33 for pain [Gross 2015]
pallof_press.dosing_recommendation: 3×10-12 reps per side with 3-5 second holds at full extension

deep_neck_flexor_training.emg_notes: Linear EMG-pressure relationship (22-30 mmHg); longus colli 17.4% CSA increase at C2-C3 [Falla 2003, Cagnie 2010]
deep_neck_flexor_training.dosing_recommendation: 10 reps × 10-second holds at each pressure level (22-30 mmHg), 2x daily for 6 weeks minimum

deadlift.emg_notes: Comparative surface-EMG studies of hamstring exercises consistently show the Romanian deadlift produces high activation of the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus, in the same tier as the good morning and glute-ham raise, with hamstring activity typically greatest during the eccentric-to-concentric transition near peak hip flexion. Relative to knee-flexion-dominant exercises (leg curl, Nordic curl), the RDL biases hip-extension-based hamstring loading and tends to emphasize the biceps femoris long head somewhat more than the semitendinosus. Erector spinae activity is substantial but predominantly isometric when a neutral spine is maintained. Gluteus maximus activation rises toward lockout as the hip approaches full extension.
deadlift.dosing_recommendation: Strength/hypertrophy: 3-4 sets of 6-10 reps at a controlled tempo, 1-2 sessions per week. For hamstring injury-risk reduction, eccentric-biased hinge work at long muscle lengths is commonly programmed 1-2x/week alongside (not replacing) high-eccentric exercises such as the Nordic hamstring curl.

grip_strengthening.emg_notes: Hand exercises reduce short-term pain (VAS -5.0) and improve grip strength (21 lbs) in hand OA [Thakker 2025]

tendon_gliding_exercises.emg_notes: FDP excursion: 23.4 mm active 4-finger mobilization vs 10.0 mm modified Kleinert [Korstanje 2012]
tendon_gliding_exercises.dosing_recommendation: 40-80 cycles per session, 4-6 sessions daily in early post-repair protocol [Tang 2021]

reverse_lunge.emg_notes: Lunge-family exercises show high activation of the quadriceps (vastus lateralis and medialis) and gluteus maximus of the lead leg, with moderate hamstring and gluteus medius activity for knee and pelvic stabilization. Biomechanical comparisons of lunge variants indicate that stepping backward keeps the lead tibia more vertical and reduces anterior translation demand and patellofemoral joint stress relative to the forward lunge, shifting relative emphasis slightly toward the hip extensors. Trunk lean forward increases gluteal and hamstring contribution; an upright trunk biases the quadriceps. Most published EMG work examines forward or walking lunges, so reverse-lunge-specific activation data are sparse and largely inferred from the broader lunge literature.
reverse_lunge.dosing_recommendation: Consistent with general resistance-training guidelines: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions per leg, 2-3 sessions per week, progressing load or depth as tolerated. For hypertrophy or strength emphasis, adjust load so the last 2-3 reps are challenging. No reverse-lunge-specific dosing trials exist; this is extrapolated from general lower-limb resistance training evidence.

maintain_ankle_mobility_and_reduce_oedem.canonical_name: Maintain ankle mobility and reduce oedema

goblet_squat.emg_notes: Goblet-squat-specific EMG studies are sparse; activation inferences come mainly from the broader squat literature. That literature consistently shows high vasti (quadriceps) activation that rises with squat depth and load, gluteus maximus activation that increases with depth, and comparatively modest hamstring activity because the hamstrings shorten at the knee while lengthening at the hip. Front-loaded squat variants shift the trunk more upright than back squats, which tends to lower lumbar extensor moment and shear while increasing anterior trunk (abdominal) bracing demand; the goblet position adds sustained isometric work for the anterior deltoid, elbow flexors, and upper trapezius to support the load. Adductor magnus contributes substantially to hip extension from deep flexion, particularly in wider stances.
goblet_squat.dosing_recommendation: For strength/hypertrophy in novice-to-intermediate trainees, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions at a moderate load (leaving 2-3 reps in reserve), 2-3 sessions per week; as a movement-prep or motor-control drill, 1-2 lighter sets of 5-8 slow, deep repetitions before lower-body training.

excessive_ir_loading_on_piriformis.canonical_name: Avoid Excessive IR Loading on Piriformis

graded_activity_return_to_normal_activit.canonical_name: Graded Activity + Return to Normal Activities

seated_row.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies of horizontal rowing variations consistently show high activation of the latissimus dorsi, middle trapezius, and rhomboid region, with meaningful biceps brachii and posterior deltoid contribution. Comparative work on rowing exercises (inverted row vs. bent-over row vs. standing cable row) indicates cable rows produce solid upper-back activation with lower lumbar spine loading than free-weight bent-over rows, making the seated cable row a common choice when spinal load must be moderated. Emphasizing full scapular retraction at end-range increases middle/lower trapezius activity, while allowing torso lean-back shifts work toward the lumbar erectors and reduces upper-back specificity. Grip orientation modestly shifts elbow-flexor emphasis (supinated favors biceps; neutral favors brachioradialis) without materially changing back activation.
seated_row.dosing_recommendation: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines for strength and hypertrophy in novice-to-intermediate trainees; loads around 60-80% 1RM taken near (not to) failure. For strength emphasis, 4-6 reps at heavier loads with longer rest.

change_of_direction_and_agility_drills.canonical_name: Change of Direction and Agility Drills

glute_bridge.emg_notes: Glute max 20-40% MVIC; hamstrings 15-25% MVIC; single-leg variation significantly increases activation [Ekstrom 2007, Hirose 2018]

barbell_bench_press.body_position: supine on flat bench, feet on floor
barbell_bench_press.emg_notes: The bench press is one of the most studied resistance exercises. Surface EMG work consistently shows high activation of the pectoralis major (both heads), anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii, with pectoralis major generally the dominant contributor on a flat bench. Incline variations shift relative activation toward the clavicular pec fibers and anterior deltoid, while decline and flat benches favor the sternocostal fibers. Narrower grips increase triceps activation and wider grips modestly increase pec activation but raise anterior shoulder stress. The sticking region occurs shortly after the chest, where mechanical leverage is poorest. Rotator cuff and scapular muscles show meaningful co-contraction for glenohumeral stability, which is why a retracted, depressed scapular set is standard coaching.
barbell_bench_press.dosing_recommendation: Strength: 3-5 sets of 3-6 reps at approximately 80-90% 1RM, 2-3 sessions per week with at least 48 hours between sessions. Hypertrophy: 3-4 sets of 6-12 reps at 65-80% 1RM taken near (but not necessarily to) failure. These ranges follow general resistance-training guidelines (e.g., ACSM position stands) applied to the bench press.

face_pull.emg_notes: Direct EMG studies of the face pull itself are sparse. Its activation profile is inferred from well-studied component patterns: horizontal abduction with external rotation produces high posterior deltoid, infraspinatus, and middle trapezius activity in EMG work on prone horizontal abduction and rowing variations, and externally rotating at the end range increases infraspinatus and teres minor demand relative to a neutral-grip row. The rope finish position biases middle and lower trapezius over upper trapezius when the athlete avoids shrugging, which is why it is commonly programmed for scapular muscle balance in overhead athletes. These inferences should not be treated as exercise-specific EMG findings for the face pull.
face_pull.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-15 repetitions, 2-3 times per week, using a load that allows full scapular retraction and external rotation without shrugging; consistent with general resistance-training guidelines for local muscular endurance and posterior shoulder strengthening.

jaw_opening_with_tongue_on_palate.canonical_name: Jaw Opening with Tongue on Palate

back_squat.emg_notes: EMG literature on the barbell squat is extensive. Vastus lateralis and vastus medialis show high activation that increases with both depth and load, and the squat is among the highest quadriceps-activating compound lifts. Gluteus maximus activation rises meaningfully with deeper squats and heavier relative loads. Hamstring activation is modest (typically well below that seen in deadlifts or Nordic exercise) because the biarticular hamstrings stay near-constant length as hip and knee flex together. Modeling and EMG work indicate the adductor magnus is a substantial hip extensor contributor in deep hip flexion. Trunk extensors (erector spinae) work at high isometric intensities to resist the flexion moment, with greater demand in low-bar and more inclined-trunk styles. Stance width mainly shifts adductor and glute contribution, with wider stances tending to increase hip musculature involvement.
back_squat.dosing_recommendation: Strength: 3-5 sets of 3-8 reps at roughly 70-85% 1RM, 2-3 sessions per week with at least 48 hours between heavy sessions; hypertrophy: 3-4 sets of 6-12 reps at moderate loads taken near failure. Consistent with general progressive resistance-training guidelines rather than squat-specific trials.

front_squat.emg_notes: Published biomechanical comparisons of the front squat versus the back squat report broadly similar EMG activation of the quadriceps, hamstrings, and lumbar erector spinae despite the front squat being performed with meaningfully lower absolute loads, alongside lower tibiofemoral compressive forces and smaller knee extensor moments at equivalent relative intensities. This makes the front squat an efficient quadriceps stimulus per unit of spinal and knee compressive load. The upright trunk position shifts demand toward the thoracic extensors and anterior core to resist the forward-flexion moment of the anteriorly racked bar, and vastus activation tends to increase with squat depth. Hamstring activity is modest and largely stabilizing rather than prime-moving.
front_squat.dosing_recommendation: For strength: 3-5 sets of 3-8 reps at roughly 70-85% 1RM, 2-3 sessions per week with at least 48 hours between sessions, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines for trained and untrained adults. For hypertrophy emphasis: 3-4 sets of 6-12 reps at moderate loads taken close to fatigue.

dumbbell_bench_press.emg_notes: The bench press is among the most-studied resistance exercises. Surface EMG work consistently shows highest activation in the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid, with the triceps brachii as the main synergist. Comparative studies of dumbbell versus barbell bench pressing generally report similar or slightly higher pectoralis major activity with dumbbells, lower triceps activity (a narrower, freer pressing path reduces elbow-extension demand), and greater demand on glenohumeral and scapular stabilizers because each arm must control its load independently, which also typically limits absolute load to below barbell equivalents. Incline positioning shifts emphasis toward the clavicular pectoralis and anterior deltoid.
dumbbell_bench_press.dosing_recommendation: General strengthening: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week on nonconsecutive days, at a load allowing 1-3 reps in reserve (consistent with ACSM resistance-training guidance). For maximal strength emphasis: 3-5 sets of 4-6 repetitions at higher loads with 2-3 minutes rest.

barbell_row.emg_notes: Published EMG comparisons of rowing variations show the bent-over barbell row produces high activation of the latissimus dorsi, middle trapezius, rhomboids, and posterior deltoid, with substantial isometric activity in the lumbar erector spinae — spine-load analyses report notably higher lumbar compression and shear in the free-standing bent-over row than in inverted or chest-supported rows, which is clinically relevant for low-back-sensitive patients. Biceps brachii and brachioradialis activity is meaningful and increases with a supinated grip; a more flared elbow shifts emphasis toward the posterior deltoid and horizontal abductors, while elbows closer to the trunk emphasize the latissimus dorsi. The upper trapezius activates to resist scapular depression/protraction under load but should not dominate the movement.
barbell_row.dosing_recommendation: General resistance-training guidelines: 2-4 sets of 6-12 repetitions at ~65-85% 1RM, 2-3 sessions per week for hypertrophy/strength; lower reps (4-6) at higher loads for strength emphasis. No condition-specific dosing evidence for this exercise beyond general strength-training recommendations.

bent_over_row.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of rowing variants (e.g., work from McGill's group comparing bent-over, inverted, and one-arm cable rows) show the bent-over row produces high activation of the latissimus dorsi, middle trapezius, and scapular retractors, together with substantial isometric thoracolumbar erector spinae activity and among the highest lumbar spine compressive loads of common rowing exercises because the trunk must be held cantilevered against the external load. Elbow flexor (biceps brachii/brachialis) activity is moderate and grip-dependent, and posterior deltoid contribution increases as the elbow path widens toward horizontal abduction. Chest-supported variants show similar upper-back activation with markedly lower spinal loading, which is the basis for using them as a regression.
bent_over_row.dosing_recommendation: For strength: 2-4 sets of 6-12 repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines (e.g., ACSM progression recommendations); progress load when all reps are completed with a stable trunk position.

lat_pulldown.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies of the lat pulldown consistently show the latissimus dorsi as the dominant mover, with substantial contributions from teres major, biceps brachii, and the middle/lower trapezius. Grip-width comparisons generally find that a medium-to-wide pronated grip produces equal or slightly greater latissimus activation than very wide or supinated grips, while supinated (underhand) grips shift more work to the biceps brachii. Pulling the bar to the front of the chest produces similar lat activation to behind-the-neck variants with less anterior shoulder stress, so the front pulldown is the standard clinical recommendation. Excessive torso lean converts the movement toward a row and increases posterior deltoid and mid-trap contribution.
lat_pulldown.dosing_recommendation: General strengthening: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions at a moderate-to-heavy load (roughly 60-80% 1RM), 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with ACSM resistance-training guidelines; hypertrophy-focused blocks may use 3-4 sets of 8-15 reps taken near volitional fatigue.

seated_cable_row.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies of horizontal rowing variations consistently show high activation of the latissimus dorsi, middle trapezius, and rhomboid region, with meaningful biceps brachii and posterior deltoid contribution. Comparative work on rowing exercises (inverted row vs. bent-over row vs. standing cable row) indicates cable rows produce solid upper-back activation with lower lumbar spine loading than free-weight bent-over rows, making the seated cable row a common choice when spinal load must be moderated. Emphasizing full scapular retraction at end-range increases middle/lower trapezius activity, while allowing torso lean-back shifts work toward the lumbar erectors and reduces upper-back specificity. Grip orientation modestly shifts elbow-flexor emphasis (supinated favors biceps; neutral favors brachioradialis) without materially changing back activation.
seated_cable_row.dosing_recommendation: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines for strength and hypertrophy in novice-to-intermediate trainees; loads around 60-80% 1RM taken near (not to) failure. For strength emphasis, 4-6 reps at heavier loads with longer rest.

pull_up.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies of the pull-up consistently show the latissimus dorsi as the most highly activated muscle, with substantial contributions from the biceps brachii and brachialis (elbow flexion) and from the lower trapezius and infraspinatus during the scapular depression and pulling phases. Grip orientation shifts emphasis: the pronated pull-up biases the latissimus dorsi and lower trapezius relative to the supinated chin-up, which shows higher biceps brachii and pectoralis major activity. Trunk musculature (rectus abdominis, obliques) works isometrically to control the hanging body. These findings come from small-sample EMG comparisons of pull-up variants in trained adults; exact percentages of MVIC vary across studies and electrode placements, so they should be read as relative rankings rather than precise values.
pull_up.dosing_recommendation: General resistance-training guidelines apply: 2-4 sets of 4-8 reps (weighted) or sets of quality body-weight reps stopping 1-2 reps short of failure, 2-3 sessions per week with at least 48 hours between sessions. No pull-up-specific dosing trials exist; this follows consensus strength-training recommendations.

chin_up.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies comparing supinated chin-ups to pronated pull-ups consistently show very high latissimus dorsi activation in both variants, with the chin-up producing greater biceps brachii and pectoralis major activity, while the pronated pull-up tends to show somewhat greater lower trapezius activity. Infraspinatus and erector spinae are also substantially active. Peak lat activity occurs through the mid-range of the pull; the dead-hang position loads the lat at long muscle length under full bodyweight distraction. These are small-sample EMG comparisons in healthy adults, so between-variant differences should be treated as tendencies rather than fixed ratios.
chin_up.dosing_recommendation: General resistance-training guidelines (not chin-up-specific trials): 2-4 sets, 2-3 sessions/week; for strength work near max effort with full recovery, for hypertrophy 6-12 quality reps or assisted variations taken close to fatigue. Progress via assistance reduction, added load, or tempo.

parallel_bar_dip.body_position: Upright, suspended between parallel bars supporting full bodyweight on the hands
parallel_bar_dip.emg_notes: Surface EMG work on dip variations shows high activation of the pectoralis major (particularly sternocostal fibers) and triceps brachii, with anterior deltoid also substantially active. Torso angle shifts the emphasis: forward lean increases pectoralis major demand while an upright torso increases relative triceps contribution. Ring dips increase stabilizer (including scapular and rotator cuff) demand compared with fixed bars. The evidence base is small — a handful of comparative EMG studies rather than the robust biomechanics literature available for barbell lifts.
parallel_bar_dip.dosing_recommendation: General resistance-training guidelines: 2-4 sets of 6-12 repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, progressing to added load once bodyweight reps are performed with control. No dip-specific dosing trials exist.

dumbbell_shoulder_press.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies comparing overhead press variations (seated vs standing, barbell vs dumbbell) consistently show the anterior deltoid as the most active muscle, with substantial middle deltoid and triceps brachii contributions. Standing and dumbbell variations tend to produce higher deltoid and trunk stabilizer activation than seated barbell pressing at matched relative loads, likely because of the greater stability demand, while allowing less absolute load. Serratus anterior and the trapezius force couple show progressively greater activity as the arms approach full overhead elevation. Rotator cuff muscles work throughout to center the humeral head, which is one reason free-weight dumbbell pressing is often preferred over machine pressing in later-stage shoulder rehabilitation.
dumbbell_shoulder_press.dosing_recommendation: For strength/hypertrophy in healthy adults, general resistance-training guidelines apply: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions at moderate-to-heavy load, 2-3 sessions per week, progressing load when all reps are completed with good form. For rotator cuff or shoulder rehab contexts, lighter loads with 10-15 repetitions and strict control are typically used before progressive loading.

lateral_raise.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of common shoulder exercises consistently show the lateral (middle) deltoid is highly active during dumbbell lateral raises — typically among the highest of common free-weight shoulder exercises for that head, generally exceeding its activation during overhead pressing. The supraspinatus is also substantially active, working with the deltoid throughout abduction rather than only in the first degrees. Anterior and posterior deltoid activity is moderate and shifts with the plane of the raise: moving into scaption biases the anterior deltoid, while staying behind the frontal plane biases the posterior fibers. Upper trapezius activity rises with the arm, particularly above roughly 60-80 degrees, and increases further if the lifter shrugs or uses momentum. Mechanically the exercise loads the deltoid most near shoulder height where the load's moment arm is longest, which is why cable variants (constant tension at the bottom) feel harder early in the range. No specific citations are attached; this summary reflects the general pattern of published EMG comparisons of deltoid exercises.
lateral_raise.dosing_recommendation: Common practice for strengthening/hypertrophy: 2-4 sets of 8-15 repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, with load selected so the last 2-3 reps are challenging while form (no trunk swing or shrug) is maintained. This follows general resistance-training guidelines rather than lateral-raise-specific trials.

biceps_curl.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies consistently show high biceps brachii activation during curls, with activation modulated by grip: a supinated grip biases biceps brachii, a neutral (hammer) grip shifts relative contribution toward brachioradialis, and a pronated grip relatively favors brachialis and brachioradialis. Curl variants that place the shoulder in extension (e.g., incline curls) load the biceps at longer muscle lengths, while preacher-style positions emphasize shorter lengths. Trunk and paraspinal activity rises in standing free-weight curls compared with seated supported versions due to the postural demand.
biceps_curl.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 repetitions, 2-3 nonconsecutive days per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines for hypertrophy/strength in novice-to-intermediate trainees; loads of roughly 60-80% 1RM or a 1-3 reps-in-reserve effort level.

hammer_curl.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of curl grip positions indicate that a neutral (hammer) grip produces relatively higher brachioradialis activation and somewhat lower biceps brachii activation than a supinated grip, because the biceps loses mechanical advantage as a supinator-flexor when the forearm is held in mid-position. The brachialis, inserting on the ulna, flexes the elbow irrespective of forearm rotation and is strongly recruited in all curl variants. Wrist flexors and extensors co-contract isometrically to keep the wrist neutral, and finger flexors work isometrically for grip. Overall the direct EMG literature on hammer curls specifically is sparse; most inferences come from studies of elbow-flexion tasks at varying forearm rotations.
hammer_curl.dosing_recommendation: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions at a moderate load (roughly 65-80% 1RM or 2-3 reps in reserve), 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines for hypertrophy and strength; no hammer-curl-specific dosing trials exist.

triceps_pushdown.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of common triceps exercises consistently show the pushdown produces high activation of the lateral and medial heads of the triceps brachii, with somewhat lower relative recruitment of the long head because the arm-at-side position keeps the biarticular long head shortened at the shoulder. Training studies comparing arm-at-side versus overhead elbow extension suggest greater long-head hypertrophy when the shoulder is flexed (long head at longer lengths), so the pushdown is best viewed as biased toward the monoarticular heads. Rope attachments allowing terminal wrist spread and full elbow lockout are commonly reported to increase peak activation near end range compared with a fixed straight bar, though differences between attachments are modest.
triceps_pushdown.dosing_recommendation: For strength/hypertrophy in healthy adults, 2-4 sets of 8-15 repetitions at moderate-to-hard effort, 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines; no pushdown-specific dosing trials exist.

skull_crusher.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of common triceps exercises show the lying triceps extension produces moderate-to-high triceps brachii activation, though generally below weighted dips, close-grip pressing, or bodyweight extensions in some comparisons. Because the shoulder is held in flexion, the long head works at a longer muscle length than in pressdown variants, and recent longitudinal work on stretch-position training suggests long-length loading of the triceps (e.g., overhead or behind-the-head variants) may favor greater long-head hypertrophy. Wrist and shoulder stabilizer activity is modest and primarily isometric.
skull_crusher.dosing_recommendation: For hypertrophy: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions at moderate load, 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines; for strength emphasis, 3-5 reps at higher load once technique is stable.

leg_extension.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies of open-chain knee extension consistently show high, well-balanced activation across the quadriceps heads. Contrary to older claims, the vastus medialis (VMO) cannot be selectively isolated from the rest of the quadriceps; VMO-to-vastus-lateralis activation ratios generally stay close to 1:1 across the range, though vastus medialis activity tends to be relatively higher in the terminal (near-full-extension) portion. Rectus femoris activation is somewhat blunted in the seated, hip-flexed position because the muscle is on relative slack. Compared with closed-chain movements like the squat, the open-chain leg extension isolates the quadriceps with minimal hamstring co-contraction. Note that peak patellofemoral joint compression occurs in the more flexed portion of the range while anterior tibiofemoral shear is greatest near terminal extension, which informs range selection in patellofemoral or ACL rehab.
leg_extension.dosing_recommendation: General resistance-training guidelines apply, as no leg-extension-specific dosing is well established: for hypertrophy roughly 3-4 sets of 8-12 reps; for muscular endurance/early rehab 2-3 sets of 12-20 reps with lighter load; train the target 2-3 times per week with about 48 hours between sessions, progressing load as tolerated. In patellofemoral rehab, limiting range to the terminal ~45-0 degrees is commonly used to reduce joint stress.

leg_curl.body_position: Prone (lying) on a leg-curl machine bench, hips and torso supported; the seated leg-curl variation places the hip in flexion with the back against a pad.
leg_curl.emg_notes: Surface-EMG studies of the leg curl consistently show high hamstring activation with position-dependent differences. Hip position shifts the emphasis: the seated (hip-flexed) leg curl tends to elicit greater overall hamstring EMG — particularly of the biarticular heads (biceps femoris long head, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) — because the hamstrings are placed on greater stretch, whereas the prone (hip-extended) curl still recruits the uniarticular biceps femoris short head robustly. Medial (semitendinosus/semimembranosus) versus lateral (biceps femoris) balance can be biased by tibial/foot rotation, and the gastrocnemius contributes as a secondary knee flexor. Reported magnitudes vary widely across studies and setups, so these are qualitative trends rather than fixed percentages.
leg_curl.dosing_recommendation: General resistance-training guidelines apply: for hypertrophy/general strength, 2-4 sets of 8-15 reps, 2-3 sessions per week with progressive overload and roughly 1-2 minutes rest between sets. No leg-curl-specific dosing protocol is established.

seated_calf_raise.emg_notes: The defining feature of the seated calf raise is knee flexion. The gastrocnemius crosses both the knee and the ankle, so flexing the knee to ~90 degrees shortens and slackens it, reducing its ability to generate force. As a result, surface EMG and biomechanical work consistently show the soleus as the dominant plantarflexor in the knee-flexed (seated) position, whereas the gastrocnemius contributes proportionally more during standing, straight-knee calf raises. The soleus is largely composed of slow-twitch (type I) fibers, which is the common rationale for training it with higher repetitions and longer time under tension. Exact activation percentages vary by study and setup and are not cited here.
seated_calf_raise.dosing_recommendation: General resistance-training guidance applies: roughly 2-3 sessions per week, about 2-4 sets of 10-20 repetitions with a controlled tempo and full range, progressing load over time. Higher rep ranges are commonly used for the soleus given its slow-twitch composition. Calf-specific dosing evidence is limited, so these are practical, expert-consensus targets rather than exercise-specific trial findings.

sit_up.emg_notes: EMG studies consistently show the sit-up is a two-phase movement: rectus abdominis and the obliques dominate the initial trunk-curl (roughly the first third of range), after which the hip flexors — psoas major, iliacus, and rectus femoris — become the primary torque producers as the trunk rises off the floor. Indwelling-EMG work has demonstrated substantial psoas activation during both bent-knee and straight-leg sit-ups, with bent knees not eliminating hip-flexor involvement as once believed. Anchoring the feet further increases hip-flexor and rectus femoris recruitment. Spine biomechanics research (notably McGill's laboratory) has measured lumbar compression during repeated full sit-ups at levels approaching occupational action limits (on the order of 3000+ N), which is the basis for preferring curl-up variations in low-back pain populations. Trunk-flexor activation in a partial curl-up is comparable to the full sit-up with markedly lower lumbar load, which is why the crunch and McGill curl-up serve as regressions rather than fundamentally different exercises.

crunch.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies consistently show the crunch produces high rectus abdominis activation and moderate external and internal oblique activation, and it compares favorably with — or exceeds — many commercial abdominal devices. Compared with a full sit-up, the shortened range keeps hip flexor (iliopsoas/rectus femoris) activity substantially lower, which is why the crunch is preferred when lumbar shear from hip flexor pull is a concern. Claims of selectively isolating the "upper" versus "lower" rectus abdominis with crunch variants are not well supported; regional differences reported across studies are small and inconsistent. Hands-behind-head performance tends to increase sternocleidomastoid recruitment if the head is pulled, which is a technique fault rather than a training target.
crunch.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-20 controlled repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines for trunk musculature; progress by adding load or lever length rather than high-repetition volume.

russian_twist.emg_notes: Surface EMG work on trunk-rotation exercises shows high activation of the external and internal obliques, with the obliques working as contralateral pairs (the external oblique opposite the turn with the internal oblique on the side of the turn). Rectus abdominis activity is moderate and largely isometric, sustaining the reclined trunk position, and it rises further when the feet are lifted. Direct EMG data on the Russian twist itself is sparse; most inferences come from studies of related rotational and curl-up-type exercises. Clinically, the combination of sustained lumbar flexion with repeated rotation under load raises disc-loading concerns in spine-biomechanics literature, so it is generally avoided or heavily modified for patients with flexion- or rotation-sensitive low back pain.
russian_twist.dosing_recommendation: No exercise-specific published dosing exists. General resistance-training guidance suggests 2-3 sets of 8-15 controlled rotations per side, 2-3 times weekly, progressing load or lever length once form is stable.

mountain_climber.body_position: high plank (prone support on hands and toes)
mountain_climber.emg_notes: Surface EMG work on plank-based dynamic core exercises shows the mountain climber elicits moderate-to-high activation of the rectus abdominis and obliques, generally exceeding a static front plank because the alternating leg drive adds anti-rotation and anti-extension perturbation. Cross-body variations tend to shift relative activation toward the obliques. Hip flexor (iliopsoas, rectus femoris) demand is high on the driving leg, and serratus anterior plus anterior deltoid are active throughout to stabilize the weight-bearing shoulder. Published EMG data specific to this exercise are limited compared with squat or deadlift literature, so these patterns are drawn from small comparative studies of plank variants and from biomechanical reasoning.

burpee.body_position: standing, transitioning through squat and prone plank each repetition
burpee.emg_notes: Formal EMG data specific to the burpee are sparse; muscle roles here are inferred from the constituent phases, each of which is well characterized: the squat and jump phases demand high quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and triceps surae activation, the plank/push-up phase loads pectoralis major, triceps brachii, anterior deltoid, and serratus anterior, and the abdominal wall and spinal extensors work isometrically to control the trunk through rapid transitions. Physiological studies of burpee interval protocols consistently show near-maximal heart rate and high oxygen-uptake responses, supporting its use as a whole-body cardiometabolic conditioning exercise more than as a targeted strengthening exercise.
burpee.dosing_recommendation: No burpee-specific dosing guideline exists; in published interval-training studies burpees are typically programmed as work-rest intervals (e.g., 20-30 s maximal effort with equal or double rest for 4-8 rounds, 2-3 sessions/week) or as 3 sets of 8-15 repetitions for general conditioning, adjusted to maintain landing mechanics.

jumping_jack.emg_notes: Published EMG data specific to jumping jacks are sparse; activation is inferred from the component motions. The out-phase demands rapid concentric hip abduction (gluteus medius/minimus, TFL) with the adductor group decelerating eccentrically, and the pattern reverses on the return, making it a light reciprocal frontal-plane conditioning drill for the hip. The calf complex (gastrocnemius/soleus) cycles between concentric propulsion and eccentric landing absorption at low amplitude, similar to submaximal hopping. The overhead arm swing recruits the deltoid with the scapular upward-rotation force couple (trapezius and serratus anterior) at moderate, rhythmic intensities. Trunk musculature works isometrically to maintain upright posture against the fast bilateral limb movement. Overall intensity per muscle is low to moderate — the exercise functions primarily as aerobic conditioning, warm-up, and low-level plyometric coordination rather than a strengthening stimulus.

jump_squat.emg_notes: Surface EMG and biomechanics studies of countermovement and jump squats show high activation of the quadriceps (vastus lateralis and medialis) and gluteus maximus during the propulsion phase, with the gastrocnemius and soleus contributing strongly in the final portion of triple extension. The hamstrings act biarticularly, assisting hip extension while transferring energy across the knee. Landing imposes large eccentric demands on the quadriceps and plantarflexors, and the tibialis anterior pre-activates prior to ground contact. Trunk musculature (erector spinae, abdominals) provides stiffness for force transfer, and gluteus medius activity is important for frontal-plane knee control, a common focus in ACL injury-prevention programs.
jump_squat.dosing_recommendation: Consistent with plyometric training guidelines: 2-3 sessions per week on non-consecutive days, 3-5 sets of 3-8 maximal-effort reps, with full recovery (60-180 s) between sets to preserve jump quality; keep total session volume modest (roughly 40-100 ground contacts) for lower-extremity plyometrics. Loaded variations for peak power development are typically performed at 0-30% of squat 1RM.

wall_sit.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies of isometric wall squats consistently show the quadriceps — particularly vastus lateralis and vastus medialis — as the dominant muscles, with activation increasing as knee flexion deepens toward 90 degrees; rectus femoris contributes less than the vasti because its hip-flexor moment is unloaded by the wall support. Hamstring co-activation is low, which is one reason the wall sit is favored when tibiofemoral shear must be limited. Gluteal and trunk-extensor activity is modest and postural. Adding an isometric ball squeeze between the knees measurably raises adductor and vastus medialis activity. Separately, isometric wall-squat training has a substantial randomized-trial literature (including meta-analyses of isometric exercise training) showing clinically meaningful reductions in resting blood pressure.
wall_sit.dosing_recommendation: For local muscular endurance: 3-5 holds of 20-60 seconds, 2-3 sessions per week, progressing hold time or load. For blood-pressure reduction, isometric exercise training trials commonly used 4 x 2-minute wall-squat holds with about 2 minutes rest, 3 sessions per week, at an individually calibrated knee angle or perceived effort.

superman.emg_notes: Surface EMG studies of prone trunk-extension exercises consistently show moderate-to-high activation of the lumbar and thoracic erector spinae and multifidus, with concurrent gluteus maximus and hamstring activity when the legs are lifted. Biomechanical modeling work (notably Stuart McGill's spine-loading research) has estimated that the full bilateral superman imposes among the highest lumbar compressive loads of common trunk-extensor exercises — on the order of several thousand newtons — which is why bird dog is generally preferred early in low-back rehabilitation and superman is reserved for asymptomatic or later-stage patients. Lifting the arms overhead in prone also produces meaningful lower trapezius and posterior deltoid activity, similar to a prone Y raise.

bear_crawl.body_position: quadruped (knees hovering, hands and toes weight-bearing)
bear_crawl.emg_notes: Direct EMG studies of the bear crawl itself are sparse; activation estimates are extrapolated from related quadruped and crawling-pattern research. Quadruped exercises with contralateral limb movement (e.g., bird-dog) show moderate activation of the multifidus, erector spinae, and abdominal obliques, and the bear crawl's reduced base of support and continuous limb exchange are expected to raise the anti-rotation demand on the obliques and transversus abdominis. Weight-bearing on the hands in a protracted, closed-chain position is a recognized stimulus for the serratus anterior, similar to push-up-plus variants. The hovering-knee position imposes a sustained isometric demand on the quadriceps and hip flexors that most plank-family exercises do not.

chest_fly.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of horizontal press and fly variations generally show high pectoralis major activation during the dumbbell fly, in a range comparable to the bench press at matched relative intensities, with substantially less triceps brachii involvement because the elbow angle is held constant. Anterior deltoid activity is moderate to high. The bottom (stretched) position places the pectoralis major under load at long muscle length, which biases mechanical tension there; it is also the position of greatest anterior shoulder stress, which motivates the limited-range floor variation for irritable shoulders. These are general findings from small EMG studies; the fly is far less studied than the bench press.
chest_fly.dosing_recommendation: 2-4 sets of 8-15 repetitions, 2x per week per general resistance-training guidelines for hypertrophy and strength; select a load leaving 1-3 reps in reserve. No fly-specific dosing trials exist.

pec_deck.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of common chest exercises have reported pectoralis major activation on the pec deck that is comparable to the barbell bench press, with lower triceps involvement since the elbow is held in a fixed, slightly flexed position. Anterior deltoid is the main synergist; posterior cuff and scapular muscles work largely as stabilizers. Because the machine constrains the movement path, it is often used clinically to isolate horizontal adduction when free-weight stabilization demands are undesirable.
pec_deck.dosing_recommendation: 2-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training guidelines for hypertrophy and strength in healthy adults; load selected so the last 2-3 reps are challenging with good form.

hanging_leg_raise.body_position: Vertical hang from overhead bar (open-chain lower body)
hanging_leg_raise.emg_notes: Comparative surface-EMG studies of abdominal exercises have measured hanging knee-up variations (including strap-supported versions) and generally report high rectus abdominis and oblique activity — among the highest of common ab exercises — along with substantial rectus femoris activity, reflecting the large hip-flexion component. Direct iliopsoas recordings are rare because the muscle is deep; its dominant role is inferred from biomechanics and fine-wire work on hip flexion tasks. Activation of the abdominals rises sharply when the pelvis is actively curled into posterior tilt at the top of the rep; without that curl the movement is predominantly hip-flexor driven with the abdominals working isometrically to fix the pelvis. Straight-leg variations are consistently more demanding than bent-knee versions due to the longer lever.
hanging_leg_raise.dosing_recommendation: 2-4 sets of 6-15 controlled repetitions, 2-3 sessions per week, consistent with general resistance-training progression guidelines; no exercise-specific dosing trials exist for this movement.

cobra_pose.emg_notes: Surface EMG work on prone trunk-extension exercises (including yoga-based studies of bhujangasana and studies of the closely related prone press-up used in McKenzie-style programs) consistently shows moderate activation of the lumbar erector spinae and multifidus, with activation rising as the chest is lifted higher and the arms contribute less. Middle/lower trapezius activity accompanies the scapular retraction-depression component, and triceps involvement scales with how much the hands press. Direct EMG data specific to cobra pose are sparse, so muscle roles here are inferred from prone-extension biomechanics and general yoga EMG literature rather than robust exercise-specific trials.
cobra_pose.dosing_recommendation: Commonly prescribed as 3-5 holds of 15-30 seconds, or 8-10 slow repetitions when performed dynamically like a press-up; this reflects clinical convention rather than trial-derived dosing.

downward_dog.body_position: quadruped / inverted-V weight-bearing on hands and feet
downward_dog.emg_notes: Small surface-EMG studies of hatha yoga poses (mostly in healthy adults, including older adults in the Yoga Empowers Seniors Study line of work) report low-to-moderate activation in downward dog: notable serratus anterior and trapezius activity from the weight-bearing upward-rotated scapula, moderate triceps and anterior deltoid activity, and modest erector spinae and abdominal activity for trunk control. Force-plate work shows roughly 55-65 percent of body weight borne through the upper limbs, which is why it is used to build wrist and shoulder weight-bearing tolerance. Hamstring and triceps surae activity is minimal — those muscles are primarily on stretch. Samples are small and protocols heterogeneous, so treat the numbers as indicative rather than definitive.
downward_dog.dosing_recommendation: Hold 20-30 seconds (about 5 slow breaths) for 3-5 repetitions, most days of the week if used for hamstring/calf flexibility — consistent with general static-stretching dosage literature (30 s holds, repeated). No pose-specific dose-response trials exist, so strengthening-oriented flow dosing is by convention rather than evidence.

worlds_greatest_stretch.body_position: standing-to-lunge (forward lunge with hands on floor, transitioning to a half-kneeling rotational reach)
worlds_greatest_stretch.emg_notes: There is no robust, exercise-specific EMG literature quantifying muscle activation for the World's Greatest Stretch, so the following is a biomechanical description rather than a measured activation profile. Actively, the drill demands low-to-moderate contraction of the trunk rotators — the obliques with assistance from the deep spinal rotators (rotatores, multifidus) and erector spinae — to produce and control the thoracic rotation, while the reaching shoulder recruits the posterior deltoid and external rotators (infraspinatus, teres minor) with lower/middle trapezius and serratus anterior stabilizing the scapula. The lumbopelvic stabilizers (transversus abdominis, quadratus lumborum) and lead-leg hip/thigh musculature (gluteus medius, quadriceps) work isometrically to hold the split-stance base. The primary intent, however, is passive/dynamic lengthening: the trailing-leg hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris), the lead-leg adductors, glutes, deep rotators (piriformis) and hamstrings, and the reaching-side pec major and latissimus dorsi are the targeted tissues placed on stretch.
worlds_greatest_stretch.dosing_recommendation: Typically programmed as part of a dynamic warm-up: about 3-5 controlled repetitions per side, moving through the range with a brief 1-2 second pause at the rotational end range, for 1-2 rounds. These figures reflect common strength-and-conditioning practice rather than a specific validated protocol; as a dynamic mobility drill it is best done after a light general warm-up and before training, not held as a long static stretch.

copenhagen_adduction.emg_notes: Adductor longus 108% MVIC (highest of all adduction exercises). Ankle support: 1.54 Nm/kg hip adductor moment vs 0.93 knee support [Serner 2014, Dæhlin 2025]
copenhagen_adduction.dosing_recommendation: Preseason: 3x/week for 6-8 weeks. In-season: 1x/week for 28 weeks. Three progression levels. High volume (2x/week) produces 24% greater strength than 1x/week [Harøy 2019, Quintana-Cepedal 2024]

side_lying_hip_adduction.emg_notes: Surface EMG comparisons of adductor exercises in athletes report high adductor longus activation for isolated side-lying hip adduction, comparable to or exceeding several functional exercises, though below the Copenhagen adduction. Adductor brevis activity is inferred from shared function and moment arm rather than measured directly, because its depth beneath adductor longus and pectineus makes surface EMG recordings unreliable and fine-wire data for this exercise are scarce.
side_lying_hip_adduction.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-15 slow, controlled repetitions per side, 3 sessions per week. Progress by adding an ankle weight or slowing the eccentric phase once 3x15 is achieved without inner-thigh fatigue before rep 12. For early groin rehab, keep pain at or below 3/10 during and after.

thumb_radial_abduction.emg_notes: The abductor pollicis longus is anatomically the prime radial abductor of the thumb, with the extensor pollicis brevis as its main assistant; formal EMG quantification specific to this isolated resisted exercise is limited.
thumb_radial_abduction.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-15 slow repetitions per hand, 3-5 days per week, with a 1-2 second hold at end range; add a light elastic band once bodyweight/gravity motion is pain-free and easy.

resisted_forearm_pronation.emg_notes: Classic EMG work indicates pronator quadratus is active during pronation independent of speed and resistance, while pronator teres contribution rises with increasing load and rotational velocity; brachioradialis participates mainly when moving from full supination toward neutral.
resisted_forearm_pronation.dosing_recommendation: Strength focus: 2-3 sets of 10-15 controlled reps per arm, 2-3 sessions per week, progressing load as form allows. For tendinopathy or early rehab, use lighter resistance with higher reps (2-3 sets of 15-20) and emphasize the pain-free range and the eccentric phase.

prone_cervical_extension.emg_notes: Deficits in cervical extensor strength and endurance are common in people with chronic neck pain, cervicogenic headache, and forward-head postures, and the deep extensors (semispinalis cervicis and multifidus) are the primary segmental stabilizers of the cervical spine. Prone extension against gravity is a simple, equipment-light way to progressively load these muscles through range. Evidence for cervical extensor and general neck-strengthening programs in chronic neck pain is moderate—systematic reviews support strengthening/endurance exercise for reducing pain and disability—but head-to-head evidence isolating this specific prone variant is limited, so it is best viewed as one reasonable loading option within a broader neck program rather than a uniquely validated technique. A neutral (chin-tucked) starting position is preferred to bias the deep extensors and avoid dumping the load into upper-cervical hyperextension.
prone_cervical_extension.dosing_recommendation: Begin with 1-2 sets of 8-10 slow repetitions or 5-10 second isometric holds, 3-4 days per week. Progress toward endurance emphasis (2-3 sets of 10-15 controlled reps or longer holds) before adding external load. Work in a pain-free to mildly-fatiguing range and avoid provoking headache or dizziness.

deep_neck_extensor_endurance.emg_notes: Surface and intramuscular EMG studies indicate that performing cervical extension with the craniocervical region held neutral-to-slightly-flexed increases activation of semispinalis cervicis relative to the superficial capitis muscles; this drives the nodded-head setup. Reported activation ratios vary between studies, so treat specifics as indicative rather than precise.
deep_neck_extensor_endurance.dosing_recommendation: Endurance emphasis: 1-3 sets of 8-12 slow repetitions with 5-10 second holds at end position, or a single sustained low-load hold building from 10 seconds. Perform daily or most days. Load stays low; stop the set when the deep muscles fatigue or the chin begins to poke forward (superficial substitution). Progress hold duration and repetitions before adding external load.

single_leg_sit_to_stand.emg_notes: Sit-to-stand is one of the best-validated functional exercises for the lower limb: performance on timed sit-to-stand tests (5-times STS, 30-second STS) reliably reflects lower-extremity strength and power and predicts fall risk in older adults, and progressive sit-to-stand training has been shown to improve leg strength, functional mobility, and gait in older and deconditioned populations. Loading a single leg substantially raises the demand on the quadriceps and hip extensors and exposes side-to-side asymmetry, which is directly relevant after knee or hip injury/surgery and for anyone who struggles to rise from low seats or climb stairs. Direct randomized evidence specifically for the single-leg variant is limited, so this is best framed as a targeted progression of a well-supported movement: the bilateral sit-to-stand evidence is moderate, and the unilateral overload rationale (closed-chain, task-specific quadriceps and gluteal strengthening with a built-in range limit) is mechanistically sound and easily dosed at home.
single_leg_sit_to_stand.dosing_recommendation: 3 sets of 5-8 controlled reps per leg, 2-3 days per week, with a 2-3 second lowering phase; rest ~60-90 seconds between sets. Progress by lowering seat height, adding external load, or shifting to eccentric-only reps as strength and control improve.

wall_angel.emg_notes: Modeled on wall-slide EMG findings showing relatively high serratus anterior and lower-trapezius activation with a low upper-trapezius-to-lower-trapezius ratio; upper trapezius should stay quiet (no shrug).
wall_angel.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-10 slow, controlled reps, 4-6 days per week; hold the top position 1-2 seconds and only work through the range you can keep full wall contact.

countertop_incline_push_up.emg_notes: Push-up EMG studies show pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii as prime movers, with serratus anterior highly active in the closed-chain hand-fixed position (especially with an added protraction 'plus'). Raising the hands (incline) reduces ground-reaction force and overall muscle activation relative to a floor push-up, providing a lower-load version of the same recruitment pattern.
countertop_incline_push_up.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 controlled repetitions, resting 60-90 seconds between sets, 2-3 non-consecutive days per week. Choose a counter height at which the last 1-2 reps feel challenging but form stays perfect and the shoulder is pain-free; progress to a lower surface once you can complete 3 sets of 12 with good control.

knee_to_wall_ankle.emg_notes: Limited ankle dorsiflexion is one of the most common mechanical restrictions after a lateral ankle sprain, in Achilles/patellar tendinopathy, and following any period of immobilization, and it drives compensations such as early heel rise, excessive foot pronation, knee valgus, and reduced squat depth. The knee-to-wall (weight-bearing lunge) position is the same posture used in the Weight-Bearing Lunge Test, which has good-to-excellent intra- and inter-rater reliability for quantifying dorsiflexion, so patients can self-measure progress in centimeters or degrees. Weight-bearing dorsiflexion self-mobilization has moderate evidence for increasing dorsiflexion ROM in people with chronic ankle instability and post-sprain, and because it loads the talocrural joint through range under body weight it targets the posterior capsule and calf tissue in a functional, closed-chain manner that transfers to gait and squatting. Because the knee is bent, gastrocnemius is slackened and the stretch/mobilization bias shifts toward soleus, the deep posterior compartment, and the joint itself rather than being a pure gastroc stretch. Evidence is graded moderate: real reliability data support the test position and there is supportive (though not definitive, largely small-trial) evidence for the mobilization improving ROM.
knee_to_wall_ankle.dosing_recommendation: Perform on the affected (or more restricted) side: 2-3 sets of 10-15 slow reps, holding 2-3 seconds at end-range contact, once or twice daily. Also usable as a pre-squat/pre-run warm-up. Work into a firm stretch or joint-tension sensation, never sharp pinch at the front of the ankle.

legs_up_the_wall.emg_notes: Predominantly a passive/restorative posture with very low muscle activation throughout; the legs are supported by the wall rather than by active contraction. No exercise-specific EMG data are established.
legs_up_the_wall.dosing_recommendation: Hold 5-15 minutes, once daily or as needed (e.g., end of day or before sleep). Come out slowly by bending the knees and rolling to one side to avoid dizziness.

wall_hamstring_stretch.emg_notes: Passive stretch with low target-muscle EMG; the hamstrings should be relaxed (minimal EMG) to allow lengthening, while light quadriceps activity may assist via reciprocal inhibition.
wall_hamstring_stretch.dosing_recommendation: Hold 30 seconds per repetition, 3-4 repetitions per leg, once or twice daily. Static holds of ~30 s are supported for ROM gains; longer or more frequent holds add little. Stretch to firm tension, never sharp pain, and breathe normally throughout.

doorway_lat_stretch.emg_notes: No exercise-specific EMG data is cited here. Mechanistically this is a passive-lengthening task: the latissimus dorsi and teres major are placed on stretch by bodyweight while the grip (finger/wrist flexors) and trunk work isometrically to hold position, so target-muscle EMG should remain low rather than showing concentric activation.
doorway_lat_stretch.dosing_recommendation: Hold 30 seconds per side, 2-3 repetitions each side, 1-2 sessions per day. Progress total hold time toward 60 seconds per side as tolerance improves; stretch to a firm but comfortable end range with no sharp anterior shoulder pain.

doorway_isometric_row.emg_notes: No EMG data specific to this doorway variant; muscle roles are inferred from rowing/scapular-retraction biomechanics.
doorway_isometric_row.dosing_recommendation: Hold 5 repetitions of 20-30 seconds at a moderate-to-high, pain-free effort (roughly 60-80 percent), resting about 30-60 seconds between holds; perform 1-2 rounds, 3-5 days per week. For symptom modulation in an irritable shoulder, start at the lower effort and shorter holds and progress as tolerated.

chair_supported_balance.emg_notes: Single-leg stance time is a validated, independent predictor of falls and all-cause decline in older adults, and progressive static/dynamic balance training is one of the best-supported interventions for reducing fall rate and fall risk in community-dwelling seniors (this is a core, evidence-backed component of programs such as Otago and multicomponent exercise, reflected in Cochrane reviews of exercise for fall prevention). Training single-leg stance also improves ankle proprioception and neuromuscular control, which reduces recurrence after lateral ankle sprain. Anchoring the drill to a chair lets a patient overload balance safely at home by regulating how much fingertip support they use — starting with light touch and weaning toward no hands — so the challenge is graded to their actual capacity rather than their fear of falling. The chair converts an otherwise high-risk task into a self-progressable home exercise, which is why it is a staple early rung in home fall-prevention and lower-limb rehab programs.
chair_supported_balance.dosing_recommendation: Hold 20-30 seconds per leg, 3-5 repetitions each side, 1-2 times daily. Progress by increasing hold time toward 30 seconds, reducing hand support, then adding the eyes-closed or head-turn variations. Always position the chair so it can be grabbed instantly if balance is lost.

tandem_stance.emg_notes: Tandem (heel-to-toe) stance is a narrowed base-of-support static balance task used to challenge and train postural control, and it is a validated rung on standardized balance measures — the Berg Balance Scale, the Short Physical Performance Battery, and the CDC STEADI progression (feet-together → semi-tandem → full tandem). Reduced tandem-stance hold time is associated with impaired balance and higher fall risk in older adults, which is why it appears in fall-risk screening. Balance and multicomponent exercise programs that include progressive static stances like this (e.g., the Otago Exercise Programme) have strong evidence from Cochrane reviews for reducing the rate of falls in community-dwelling older adults. As an isolated drill the specific RCT support is more limited, but the mechanistic rationale is sound: narrowing the base loads the ankle and hip frontal-plane stabilizers and forces integration of somatosensory, vestibular, and visual input for standing balance. Practical indications include fall-prevention programs, lower-limb proprioceptive deficits, ankle instability, and general balance retraining.
tandem_stance.dosing_recommendation: Hold the tandem position for 30 seconds, then switch which foot is forward; 3-4 holds per side, 1-2 times per day. Progress hold time or advance to a harder variation once you can hold 30 seconds steadily without touching support.

heel_to_toe_walk.emg_notes: No exercise-specific EMG data cited; muscle roles are assigned from gait and postural-control biomechanics (narrowed base of support increases frontal-plane hip abductor and ankle evertor/invertor demand).
heel_to_toe_walk.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-20 heel-to-toe steps, once or twice daily. Rest as needed between sets and always work within arm's reach of a wall or counter until steady.

desk_wrist_flexor_stretch.emg_notes: Primarily a passive stretch: the wrist and finger flexors (flexor carpi radialis/ulnaris, flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, palmaris longus) are under lengthening tension with minimal volitional activation, while the wrist extensors act only lightly to position or hold the joint when the stretch is taken actively. No high-force muscle work is intended.
desk_wrist_flexor_stretch.dosing_recommendation: Hold 20-30 seconds, 2-4 repetitions per side, 2-3 times per day; a good micro-break to repeat hourly during long desk sessions. Stretch to a gentle, tolerable pull with no pain or nerve symptoms.

desk_wrist_extensor_stretch.emg_notes: Targets the common wrist/finger extensor group (notably extensor carpi radialis brevis) whose enthesis at the lateral epicondyle is the pain source in lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow), and which becomes tight and symptomatic with sustained desk/keyboard and gripping work. Restoring extensor and posterior-forearm extensibility is a standard component of multimodal conservative care for lateral epicondylalgia and generic forearm/wrist overuse, and it is trivially self-administered at a desk for adherence. Honest evidence appraisal: stretching as an isolated intervention has only limited high-quality support — the strongest evidence for lateral epicondylalgia favors progressive loading (eccentric/heavy-slow resistance of the wrist extensors), with stretching typically studied as an adjunct within combined programs rather than a stand-alone cure. The defensible rationale here is mechanistic and functional (reduce extensor tension, provide symptom relief and a movement break during prolonged static desk postures), so it is best positioned as a low-risk complement to strengthening, not a substitute.
desk_wrist_extensor_stretch.dosing_recommendation: Hold 30 seconds per repetition, 3-4 repetitions, 2-3 times per day. Stretch to mild tension only (no sharp or nerve-like pain); can be done as a microbreak during prolonged desk/keyboard work.

towel_row.emg_notes: This is a self-regulated horizontal pulling exercise that lets a patient train the scapular retractors and posterior shoulder at home with no equipment beyond a towel and a door. Horizontal rowing is a well-studied way to load the middle and lower trapezius, rhomboids, and posterior deltoid: surface-EMG work on rowing variations consistently shows high activation of these scapular stabilizers, which is the rationale for including rows in programs for scapular dyskinesis, postural (upper-crossed) presentation, and general shoulder-girdle conditioning. Strengthening these muscles helps counterbalance dominant, often-tight anterior chest musculature and supports the balanced force-couples that upwardly rotate and stabilize the scapula. The row pattern itself has moderate published support; the specific towel-on-a-door variant has no dedicated trials, so its value rests on the transferable EMG/strengthening evidence for rowing plus its practical merit as an accessible, infinitely scalable home substitute for a band or cable row. It is a sound entry-level or bridge exercise, not a maximal-load one, because a towel/door caps the achievable resistance.
towel_row.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-15 controlled reps, resting about 60 seconds between sets, 2-3 days per week; adjust foot position so the last 2-3 reps of each set feel challenging but form stays clean.

towel_scapular_retraction.body_position: seated or standing, upright with a neutral spine
towel_scapular_retraction.emg_notes: Isometric outward pull on the towel biases the middle/lower trapezius and rhomboids while keeping upper-trapezius activity low if shrugging is avoided; cueing scapular depression helps favor a lower-trap over upper-trap recruitment ratio.
towel_scapular_retraction.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-15 repetitions with a 3-5 second hold at end range, once daily or most days of the week; progress by increasing pull effort or hold time as the squeeze becomes easy and pain-free.

stair_calf_raise.emg_notes: Standing heel raises produce high gastrocnemius and soleus activation; the straight-knee position biases the gastrocnemius while a slightly flexed knee shifts emphasis to the soleus. Peronei and deep posterior compartment (tibialis posterior, long toe flexors) act as synergists/stabilizers, more so on the unstable step edge.
stair_calf_raise.dosing_recommendation: General strengthening: 3 sets of 12-15 controlled reps (2-3 s up, brief hold, 2-3 s lower below the step), 4-5 days per week, progressing to single-leg or added load. Achilles tendinopathy (eccentric emphasis): work toward 3 sets of 15 heel drops, twice daily, per the Alfredson protocol, using mild-to-moderate tolerable discomfort as the guide.

eccentric_stair_descent.emg_notes: Descent phase is quadriceps-dominant and eccentric: the vasti and rectus femoris show high activity while lengthening to control knee flexion, with the loaded supporting leg carrying most of the demand. Gluteus medius activity rises to control frontal-plane knee position on the single stance leg, and gastroc/soleus and tibialis anterior modulate to control tibial progression and foot placement.
eccentric_stair_descent.dosing_recommendation: 3 sets of 8-12 controlled step-downs per leg (each rep 3-4 seconds lowering), 4-6 days/week. In tendinopathy rehab, work into acceptable discomfort (roughly ≤4/10 pain that settles by the next morning) and progress load gradually over 8-12 weeks.

backpack_weighted_carry.emg_notes: This is a functional loaded-carry (gait-under-load) task that trains the whole postural chain to resist fatigue while walking — directly transferable to daily activities like carrying groceries, a child, or luggage. The mechanistic and clinical basis is well established even where carry-specific trials are limited: (1) added axial/weighted-walking load is an osteogenic stimulus, and weighted-vest walking programs have shown benefit for bone-mineral density and postural strength in older and postmenopausal adults, so a graded weighted backpack is a low-cost home proxy; (2) walking with an anteriorly-compensated posterior load imposes sustained isometric demand on the spinal erectors, quadratus lumborum, and deep abdominal stabilizers, building the trunk-endurance that is repeatedly associated with reduced low-back-pain risk (McGill's endurance work); and (3) gait under load recruits the hip extensors and abductors for single-leg-stance control, supporting balance and lower-limb power relevant to fall prevention. It is scalable simply by changing pack weight, distance, or pace, which makes it practical for progressive home dosing. Evidence for the general strategy is moderate; evidence for the backpack specifically is more limited and mechanistic, so it is rated limited here.
backpack_weighted_carry.dosing_recommendation: 10–20 minutes of continuous walking, 2–4 sessions per week. Begin with a light load (roughly 5–10% of body weight or whatever keeps posture tall) and progress load, time, or terrain gradually as tolerated. Stop or lighten if posture collapses forward or low-back/shoulder discomfort arises.

water_bottle_lateral_raise.emg_notes: Lateral raises produce high middle-deltoid activation (commonly >50–70% MVIC near shoulder height) with substantial supraspinatus involvement; upward-rotator activity (serratus anterior, upper/lower trapezius) rises with elevation angle. Peak deltoid demand occurs around 80–90° of abduction.
water_bottle_lateral_raise.dosing_recommendation: 2–3 sets of 12–15 controlled reps, light load (e.g. 500 mL bottles ≈ 0.5 kg each), 30–60 s rest between sets, 2–3 sessions per week. Keep the range pain-free and stop short of any pinching arc.

prone_press_up.emg_notes: This is the core end-range extension exercise of the McKenzie Method (Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy) for low back pain. It is indicated for patients with a directional preference for extension — those whose leg or back symptoms centralize (move from the leg/buttock toward the midline of the spine) with repeated lumbar extension, a pattern classically seen with discogenic/derangement-type pain. Randomized and cohort evidence supports classifying LBP by directional preference and matching treatment to it: patients treated with their preferred direction show better pain and function outcomes than mismatched or general exercise. The mechanism proposed is a reduction of flexion-biased mechanical stress and, over repeated end-range loading, symptom centralization, which is itself a favorable prognostic sign. It is a safe, self-administered home tool that lets patients self-manage flare-ups. Evidence is graded moderate: real trial support exists for the MDT/directional-preference approach, but effects are specific to the correctly classified subgroup, and extension is contraindicated where symptoms peripheralize or in extension-sensitive presentations (e.g., spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis).
prone_press_up.dosing_recommendation: Typically 10 repetitions per set, holding the top position 1-2 seconds, repeated roughly every 2-3 hours (about 6-8 sessions per day) during an acute extension-responsive episode; reduce frequency as symptoms centralize and resolve.

hollow_body_hold.emg_notes: Dished, long-lever supine holds elicit high rectus abdominis and oblique activation; abdominal EMG rises as the arm/leg levers lengthen and the legs are lowered toward the floor, while erector spinae stays relatively quiet as an isometric anti-extension task.
hollow_body_hold.dosing_recommendation: Hold 20-30 seconds for 3-4 sets, resting 45-60 seconds between; progress by adding time (up to ~45-60 s) or lengthening the limb levers before adding sets. Perform 3-4 days per week. Stop or regress the moment the low back lifts off the floor.

bodyweight_hip_hinge.emg_notes: Hip-dominant hinging preferentially recruits gluteus maximus and the hamstring group as prime movers while the erector spinae and multifidus act isometrically to hold a neutral spine; deeper hinge angles increase posterior-chain (hamstring/glute) activation relative to a squat pattern.
bodyweight_hip_hinge.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 controlled reps, 3-4 days/week; focus on quality of the neutral-spine pattern rather than fatigue. A 2-3 second lowering (eccentric) phase reinforces motor control.

wall_sit_isometric.emg_notes: Sustained submaximal quadriceps activation dominates, with vastus medialis and vastus lateralis showing rising EMG amplitude and progressive motor-unit recruitment as the hold continues and fatigue accumulates; deeper knee angles and single-leg variants raise activation. Gluteus maximus and hamstrings show lower-level co-contraction for hip and knee stabilization.
wall_sit_isometric.dosing_recommendation: Blood-pressure protocol: 4 holds of 2 minutes at a moderate intensity (about knee angle giving a hard-but-sustainable effort), with 2 minutes rest between holds, 3 sessions per week for at least 8 to 12 weeks.
