Strengthening/knee-pain protocol: 3 to 5 holds of 30 to 60 seconds, 1 to 2 minutes rest, most days of the week; progress hold time and depth as tolerated. Stop a hold if knee pain exceeds a mild 3/10 or if you cannot keep breathing normally.

doorframe_calf_stretch.emg_notes: No exercise-specific EMG data cited; muscle roles are assigned from functional anatomy of ankle dorsiflexion placing the posterior compartment plantarflexors on stretch.
doorframe_calf_stretch.dosing_recommendation: Hold 30 seconds (build to 45-60 s for tight calves), 3-4 repetitions per leg, once or twice daily. Stretch to a firm but comfortable pull, never sharp pain. Perform both the straight-knee (gastrocnemius) and bent-knee (soleus) variations. A common protocol is 3 x 30 s per side, 2-3 times per day, especially before first steps in the morning for plantar heel pain.

countertop_supported_squat.emg_notes: A supported squat trains the same sit-to-stand pattern that predicts functional independence: repeated closed-chain knee and hip extension builds lower-limb strength and power, which is strongly associated with reduced fall risk and easier chair/toilet transfers in older and deconditioned adults. The countertop provides an upper-limb "handhold" that lets a patient who cannot yet do a free-standing squat or unsupported sit-to-stand still load the quadriceps and glutes safely, then progressively wean off the arms as strength returns — a graded loading strategy well supported for knee osteoarthritis, post-surgical quad weakness, and general frailty/sarcopenia. Evidence for progressive resistance and sit-to-stand-style training improving lower-limb strength and physical function in older adults is robust; the specific "hands on counter" regression is standard clinical practice rather than a separately trialed protocol, so it is rated moderate.
countertop_supported_squat.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 repetitions, controlled tempo (about 2 seconds down, 2 seconds up), 3-4 days per week. Progress by reducing hand support before adding range, tempo, or reps. Work within a pain-free or mild (≤3/10) range for knee OA or post-surgical cases.

chair_triceps_dip.body_position: seated-supported (hands on chair edge, hips off seat, weight through arms)
chair_triceps_dip.emg_notes: Dip-pattern pressing is among the highest triceps brachii activators on surface EMG; anterior deltoid and clavicular pectoralis major contribute during the shoulder-flexion drive, while lower trapezius and serratus anterior act isometrically to keep the scapula depressed and stable.
chair_triceps_dip.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 controlled repetitions, 2-3 times per week, resting 60-90 seconds between sets; use a range of motion that stays pain-free at the front of the shoulder.

bird_dog_elbow_knee.emg_notes: The static bird dog shows moderate multifidus and erector spinae activation (commonly ~20-40% MVIC in EMG studies) at relatively low lumbar compressive load; the elbow-knee flexion phase adds rectus abdominis and oblique activation not seen in the static hold. Values for this specific dynamic variant are not well characterized in the literature.
bird_dog_elbow_knee.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 controlled reps per side, alternating or completing one side before switching. Move slowly (about 2-3 s per phase), pause briefly at the level reach, and stop a set if you can no longer keep the pelvis square and spine neutral. Perform most days as part of a core motor-control routine.

prone_ytw_raise.emg_notes: Prone arm raises at these angles are used specifically to bias the lower and middle trapezius and posterior rotator cuff while keeping upper-trapezius activity low (favorable lower-trap/upper-trap ratio). The 'thumbs up, no shrug, lead with the shoulder blade' cueing is what shifts activation toward the intended stabilizers; letting the shoulders shrug recruits the upper trapezius and defeats the purpose.
prone_ytw_raise.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 slow repetitions of the full Y-T-W sequence (or per letter), with a 2-second hold at the top of each position, performed 3-4 days per week. Progress by lengthening the holds before adding light external load.

standing_hip_abduction_support.emg_notes: Standing/weight-bearing hip abduction produces moderate gluteus medius activation but generally lower than side-lying abduction, side-plank, and banded lateral-walk variants in comparative EMG studies; activation increases with added band or ankle-weight resistance and when the toes are kept forward to reduce TFL substitution.
standing_hip_abduction_support.dosing_recommendation: 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 repetitions per leg, performed slowly (about 2 seconds up, 2 seconds down), 3 to 4 days per week. Progress by adding a band or ankle weight once 15 controlled reps are easy with a level pelvis.

stair_edge_calf_raise.emg_notes: This trains the plantarflexors (gastrocnemius/soleus) and loads the Achilles tendon through a large range, including the lengthened position as the heel drops below the step edge — something a flat-floor heel raise cannot achieve. Plantarflexor strength and calf-muscle capacity are prime movers of gait push-off, running, jumping, and stair negotiation, and they decline markedly with age; low plantarflexor strength is associated with slower gait speed and reduced balance/fall resilience in older adults. Progressive heel-raise programs reliably increase plantarflexor strength and calf muscle volume, and full-range/eccentric heel-drop loading off a step is a cornerstone of rehabilitation for Achilles (mid-portion) tendinopathy, where the Alfredson eccentric heel-drop and heavy-slow-resistance calf protocols have solid trial support for reducing pain and improving function. Evidence level set to moderate: strong support exists for calf loading in Achilles tendinopathy and for plantarflexor strengthening generally, though the specific stair-edge dose varies across studies.
stair_edge_calf_raise.dosing_recommendation: 3 sets of 12-15 reps, 3-4x/week, with a controlled ~2-3 s lower and a brief pause in the stretched bottom position; progress to single-leg or added load as tolerated. For Achilles tendinopathy, a higher-volume eccentric heel-drop scheme (e.g., 3x15 twice daily) may be used under guidance.

towel_hamstring_curl.emg_notes: This is a home-friendly way to load the hamstrings eccentrically — the same training stimulus behind eccentric knee-flexor programs. Eccentric hamstring strengthening (best studied as the Nordic hamstring exercise) has strong RCT and meta-analytic support for reducing hamstring strain injury incidence in athletes and for building fascicle length and eccentric strength, both linked to injury risk. The towel/slider curl is a lower-load, easily scalable regression of that principle: it lets a patient train the hip-hinge-into-knee-flexion eccentric pattern early in rehab or before they can tolerate a full Nordic, using only a towel and floor. It is a good indication for hamstring strain rehab, posterior-chain endurance, and as a bridge toward Nordic curls. Honest caveat: the specific towel/slider variant has limited direct trial evidence — its support is extrapolated from the well-studied eccentric hamstring literature and from EMG showing high hamstring activation in slider/bridge curls — so I have set the evidence level to moderate rather than strong.
towel_hamstring_curl.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 6-10 controlled reps, emphasizing a slow 3-5 second eccentric slide-out, 2-3 times per week on non-consecutive days. Progress by adding range, reps, or moving to single-leg once form and hip height are maintained without low-back strain.

wall_ball_squat.emg_notes: This is primarily a closed-chain quadriceps builder that patients can do safely at home with almost no equipment. Quadriceps strengthening is one of the best-supported conservative interventions for knee osteoarthritis and patellofemoral pain, and the wall squat keeps the trunk supported so load can be dosed by squat depth and hold time — useful when balance, pain, or deconditioning limit a free-standing squat. The mid-range wall position also keeps patellofemoral joint stress moderate, which is why it is a common early-stage knee rehab choice. Separately, the isometric wall sit/wall squat has emerging support for lowering resting blood pressure: a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in a sports-medicine journal found isometric exercise training — with wall squats among the most effective modes — produced meaningful reductions in resting systolic and diastolic pressure. Evidence is set to moderate: quad strengthening for knee pain is strongly supported, and the blood-pressure benefit is promising but from a smaller, still-maturing body of trials.
wall_ball_squat.dosing_recommendation: Strengthening: 3-5 sets of 30-45 second holds at a tolerable knee angle, or 3 sets of 10-15 slow reps, most days of the week. Blood-pressure protocol: 4 x 2-minute holds near 90-135 degrees of knee flexion with 1-2 minutes rest, ~3 sessions per week. Progress by increasing depth, hold time, or advancing to single-leg. Stay within pain-free range.

stair_step_up.emg_notes: Lead-limb quadriceps (vasti and rectus femoris) and gluteus maximus show the highest activation during the concentric lift; gluteus medius activity rises during single-leg loading to control pelvic drop. Higher step heights and slower eccentric lowering increase quadriceps and gluteal EMG demand.
stair_step_up.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 repetitions per leg, 2-3 times per week; rest about 60-90 seconds between sets. Start with the bottom step and light hand support, progressing height and load as control and strength improve.

seated_knee_extension.emg_notes: Vastus medialis activity increases toward terminal extension, supporting the end-range hold; rectus femoris contribution is relatively reduced in sitting because the flexed hip shortens it (active insufficiency).
seated_knee_extension.dosing_recommendation: 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 repetitions per leg, with a 2-second hold at end range, most days of the week; progress load or reps once the target range is completed without fatigue or knee pain.

standing_calf_stretch_step.emg_notes: This is a passive/gravity-driven static stretch, so target muscle EMG activity should stay low; the posterior calf (gastrocnemius, soleus) is under passive tension rather than active contraction. Excessive gripping or high plantarflexor EMG during the hold indicates the patient is guarding and should be cued to relax and let body weight lower the heel.
standing_calf_stretch_step.dosing_recommendation: Hold each stretch 30 seconds, 3-4 repetitions per leg, doing both a knee-straight (gastrocnemius) and a slightly knee-bent (soleus) hold. Perform once or twice daily; accumulating roughly 2-3 minutes per calf per session is a reasonable target. Stretch to gentle tension, never sharp pain, and ease off if there is nerve tingling or numbness in the foot.

active_anterior_pelvic_tilt.emg_notes: Not based on exercise-specific EMG data; muscle roles are assigned from anatomical action (lumbar extensors and anterior hip flexors as prime movers of anterior pelvic tilt, abdominals and gluteals as their lengthening antagonists). Treat activation claims as anatomically reasoned, not EMG-verified.
active_anterior_pelvic_tilt.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-12 slow, controlled repetitions, or 8-10 reps with a brief 2-3 second hold at end range. Can be done daily as a mobility/awareness drill or used as a warm-up. Progress by increasing range, adding the hold, or advancing to quadruped/standing variations as control improves.

pelvic_clock_mobilization.emg_notes: No specific surface-EMG validation exists for this drill; muscle roles listed are mechanistic/anatomical inferences rather than EMG-confirmed activation levels.
pelvic_clock_mobilization.dosing_recommendation: 1-2 sets of 5-8 slow circles in each direction (or 8-10 controlled tilts per direction for the two-point version), once daily or as a warm-up/awareness primer before core and hip-hinge work. Motion should be small, smooth, and pain-free; quality over quantity.

standing_hip_hike.emg_notes: Surface-EMG studies of pelvic-drop / hip-hike variations report substantial gluteus medius activation on the standing leg, often in the same range as, or higher than, common side-lying and standing abduction drills, supporting its use for hip-abductor strengthening. Quantitative EMG specific to quadratus lumborum during the hike is sparse, so its role is inferred anatomically. Activation magnitudes vary with step height, load, and how strictly trunk lean is controlled.
standing_hip_hike.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-15 controlled repetitions per side, roughly 3 times per week. Emphasize a slow, controlled lowering phase and full but pain-free range. Progress by adding load or step height once 15 clean reps per side feel easy.

cervical_protraction_awareness.emg_notes: No EMG data specific to this awareness drill. By movement pattern, sternocleidomastoid and scalene activity accompany the forward glide while the deep cervical flexors (longus colli/capitis) go relatively quiet, which is the functional rationale for using the return-to-neutral phase to re-cue deep-flexor control.
cervical_protraction_awareness.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 8-10 slow, controlled repetitions, holding 2-3 seconds at the forward and neutral positions, once or twice daily. Movement should be smooth and pain-free; stop short of any range that provokes symptoms.

upper_cervical_rotation_drill.emg_notes: Roughly 45-50% of total cervical rotation occurs at a single joint, the atlanto-axial (C1-C2) segment, and pre-positioning the neck in upper-cervical flexion (a chin nod) biomechanically limits rotation of the lower segments so that movement is concentrated there. This is the same principle behind the cervical flexion-rotation test, which has good reliability and diagnostic validity for identifying upper-cervical rotation restriction, particularly in cervicogenic headache populations. That diagnostic evidence is stronger than the evidence that a self-administered rotation drill measurably improves range or symptoms: direct trial evidence for this specific exercise is limited and largely extrapolated from manual-therapy and general neck-mobility studies. The honest framing is mechanistic and low-risk — it targets a real, commonly under-mobilized segment and offers a body-awareness benefit — rather than a claim of proven outcomes. It is appropriate as an accessible mobility and awareness drill for people who never train fine neck movement, and it should be pain-free and free of dizziness; symptoms such as dizziness, nausea, or visual disturbance are a reason to stop and seek assessment.
upper_cervical_rotation_drill.dosing_recommendation: Perform 1-2 sets of 5-8 slow rotations per side, once or twice daily. Move only within a pain-free, dizziness-free range; quality and control matter more than range or repetitions. Stop and reassess if you feel dizziness, nausea, visual changes, or arm symptoms.

seated_cervical_flexion_arom.emg_notes: No exercise-specific EMG data referenced; muscle roles are assigned from functional anatomy of cervical flexion rather than measured activation.
seated_cervical_flexion_arom.dosing_recommendation: Perform 5-10 slow, controlled repetitions, 1-3 times per day, moving only within a comfortable, pain-free range. Optionally hold end range 3-5 seconds. Stop and reassess if the movement provokes dizziness, radiating symptoms, or increasing pain.

upper_cervical_extension_control.emg_notes: No exercise-specific EMG data is cited here; the suboccipital muscles are deep and small and are not readily or reliably captured by surface EMG, so muscle roles are assigned from applied anatomy and kinematics rather than measured activation.
upper_cervical_extension_control.dosing_recommendation: Start with 1-2 sets of 8-10 slow, controlled reps, once or twice daily, prioritizing quality over quantity. Progress toward 2-3 sets and add 3-5 second end-range holds as control improves. Stop the set if fatigue causes the lower neck to take over or any symptoms appear.

radial_deviation_strengthening.emg_notes: Radial deviation is produced by the radial wrist muscles co-contracting: the flexor carpi radialis and extensor carpi radialis longus pull the hand thumb-ward while their opposing flexion/extension moments largely cancel, with contributions from the thumb's radial abductors/extensors (abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis/longus). Strengthening it is grounded primarily in wrist anatomy and long-standing clinical practice rather than a large body of trial evidence — direct randomized trials on isolated radial deviation strengthening in healthy people are sparse, so the evidence is best described as limited/mechanistic. It is a reasonable, low-risk addition for building balanced wrist strength, addressing a commonly under-trained direction, and supporting demands like racket/club sports and tool use. One honest caution: because radial deviation loads the first dorsal compartment tendons (APL/EPB), it should be introduced gently and is often modified or deferred in people with De Quervain's-type radial wrist pain.
radial_deviation_strengthening.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 12-15 slow, controlled reps per wrist, 2-3 times per week. Start with a very light load (1-3 lb or a light band) and progress load only when the full range is smooth and pain-free. Rest ~60 seconds between sets.

ulnar_deviation_strengthening.emg_notes: Ulnar deviation is produced primarily by a force couple between the flexor carpi ulnaris (palm side) and extensor carpi ulnaris (back side) pulling the wrist toward the little finger. These muscles are also key dynamic stabilizers of the ulnar wrist and the distal radioulnar joint, so building capacity here is commonly used in rehab for TFCC irritation, ulnar-sided wrist pain, and general wrist/grip conditioning. Direct high-quality trial evidence for isolated ulnar deviation strengthening as a standalone intervention is limited; the strongest support is anatomical and biomechanical, plus its inclusion in broader wrist-strengthening and grip programs. It is best viewed as a low-risk accessory movement grounded in muscle function rather than a treatment with its own robust outcome data. Progressive resistance and specificity principles (train the motion you want to strengthen) reasonably apply. Load should stay light because the moment arm is short and the deviator muscles are small.
ulnar_deviation_strengthening.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 12-15 slow, controlled reps per wrist, performed 3-4 days per week. Use a light load (often 1-3 lb to start) that keeps the last 2-3 reps challenging but pain-free; progress load or lever length gradually once the target reps feel easy and symptom-free.

dart_throwers_motion.emg_notes: The dart-thrower's motion (DTM) is one of the best-described planes in wrist biomechanics. Kinematic and cadaveric studies (e.g., work by Moritomo, Crisco, Wolfe and colleagues) show it is the functional plane the wrist uses for most power and precision tasks, and that during DTM the proximal carpal row (scaphoid and lunate) moves comparatively little while most motion occurs at the midcarpal joint. Because of this, DTM places relatively low strain across the scapholunate interval, which is the rationale for its wide use as an early, protected rehabilitation motion after scapholunate ligament injury, distal radius fracture, and scaphoid fracture/repair. The biomechanical evidence for the movement itself is strong; the evidence that DTM-based rehab improves clinical outcomes versus standard cardinal-plane exercise is still limited and largely drawn from small studies and expert consensus, so it is best framed as a biomechanically-grounded, well-reasoned choice rather than a proven superior protocol. For the general population it is valuable simply as a commonly untrained, real-world plane of wrist motion that builds coordinated control most people never practice in isolation.
dart_throwers_motion.dosing_recommendation: 2-3 sets of 10-15 slow, controlled repetitions, once daily or every other day. In a rehab context, begin pain-free and within a protected range as guided by the treating clinician, then progress range, load, and speed as tolerated.

wrist_circles_arom.emg_notes: Active range-of-motion (AROM) exercises like wrist circles are a long-standing, low-risk staple of rehabilitation used to preserve joint mobility, promote synovial fluid movement, and reduce stiffness, particularly early after injury or immobilization when loading is not yet appropriate. The mechanistic reasoning is sound and clinically accepted: moving a joint through its available range maintains capsular and tendon excursion and provides sensory input without imposing significant load. However, the direct evidence for wrist circles specifically is limited. There are no high-quality randomized trials isolating this drill; support comes largely from clinical convention, expert consensus, and extrapolation from broader AROM and early-mobilization literature. AROM is best understood as a mobility-maintenance and symptom-management tool rather than a driver of strength or lasting range gains, which typically require progressive loading or sustained stretching. Circumduction should stay within a pain-free arc; it is not a treatment for acute wrist fractures, unstable joints, or conditions where motion is contraindicated without clearance.
wrist_circles_arom.dosing_recommendation: Perform 8 to 12 slow circles in each direction, 1 to 3 sets, once or twice daily. Use as a warm-up before wrist or grip activity, or as a movement break during prolonged static hand postures. Keep all motion within a pain-free range; mild stretch is acceptable, sharp pain is not.
